---
title: "Build a repeatable local development workflow"
date: 2026-04-12
categories: [development]
tags: [local-dev, ddev, taskfile, direnv]
summary: "Set up a local development workflow that starts fast, stays consistent, and is easy for your team to verify."
slug: "build-a-repeatable-local-development-workflow"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to build a repeatable local development workflow with [DDEV](https://ddev.com/), [Task](https://taskfile.dev/), and [direnv](https://direnv.net/) so your project starts the same way on every machine.

## Prerequisites

- [Git](https://git-scm.com/)
- [Docker](https://www.docker.com/)
- [DDEV](https://ddev.com/)
- [Task](https://taskfile.dev/)
- [direnv](https://direnv.net/)

## Map Your Local Development Workflow

A good local workflow has one job: make the right thing the easy thing. You should be able to clone the repo, allow the environment, start services, and run the app without guessing. That sounds simple, but the handoff between tools is where teams usually lose time.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Clone repo] --> B[Allow direnv]
    B --> C[Load local environment variables]
    C --> D[Run task setup]
    D --> E[DDEV starts containers]
    E --> F[Task commands run inside the project workflow]
    F --> G[Verify app, tests, and checks]
```

This flow gives you one path into the project. The rest of the post turns each step into something you can keep in the repo.

## Put Project Commands In Taskfile.yml

Start by moving your common commands into a `Taskfile.yml`. That gives you short, named entry points for setup, startup, tests, and cleanup.

```yaml
version: '3'

tasks:
  setup:
    desc: Prepare the project for first use
    cmds:
      - ddev start
      - ddev exec composer install
      - ddev exec npm install

  dev:
    desc: Start the local app services
    cmds:
      - ddev start
      - ddev launch

  test:
    desc: Run the test suite
    cmds:
      - ddev exec php artisan test

  lint:
    desc: Run code quality checks
    cmds:
      - ddev exec vendor/bin/pint --test

  reset:
    desc: Rebuild the local environment
    cmds:
      - ddev restart
```

This file gives your project stable command names. Instead of remembering a chain of shell commands, you run `task setup`, `task dev`, or `task test`, but those commands still depend on the right environment loading first.

## Load Local Defaults With direnv

Use `direnv` to load project-specific environment variables when you enter the directory. That keeps local defaults close to the code and removes one more setup step from memory.

```bash
export COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=myapp
export APP_ENV=local
export DDEV_ROUTER_HTTP_PORT=8080
export DDEV_ROUTER_HTTPS_PORT=8443
```

Put that in `.envrc` at the project root. When you run `direnv allow`, those values load automatically every time you `cd` into the repo, which makes your task commands more predictable.

If your team needs a safe starting point, keep an example file in the repo too.

```bash
cp .envrc.example .envrc
direnv allow
```

That gives new contributors a working baseline without forcing them to read a setup document line by line. The environment is ready, but the container layer still needs a stable project definition.

## Keep DDEV Configuration In The Repo

Your local container setup should live in version control. That includes the project type, web root, runtime version, and any extra services your app needs.

```yaml
name: myapp
type: php
php_version: "8.3"
webserver_type: nginx-fpm
docroot: public
xdebug_enabled: false
additional_hostnames: []
additional_fqdns: []
database:
  type: mariadb
  version: "10.11"
```

Put that in `.ddev/config.yaml`. It tells DDEV how to build the local environment, so one developer does not end up on a different stack than everyone else.

If you need extra services, add them beside the main config instead of documenting them in prose.

```yaml
services:
  mailpit:
    image: axllent/mailpit:latest
    ports:
      - "8025:8025"
```

This kind of definition makes the dependency visible and repeatable. Once the repo owns the environment, you can focus on the order people should actually use it.

## Use A Single Onboarding Path

Do not make readers assemble the workflow themselves. Give them one path that works for first-time setup and day-to-day use.

{{< steps >}}
{{< step "Clone and enter the project" >}}
Clone the repository and move into the project directory so `direnv` can detect `.envrc`.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Allow the environment" >}}
Run `direnv allow` once. After that, the project variables load automatically when you enter the directory.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Run setup" >}}
Run `task setup` to start DDEV and install project dependencies.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Start daily work" >}}
Run `task dev` for normal development and `task test` before you commit.
{{< /step >}}
{{< /steps >}}

That sequence is short enough to remember. It also gives you a clean place to add verification so the workflow proves itself.

## Verify The Workflow On A Fresh Shell

A local workflow is only useful if it works outside your current shell history. Test it the same way a new contributor would.

```bash
direnv reload
task setup
task test
```

`direnv reload` confirms the environment still resolves cleanly. `task setup` and `task test` prove that your startup path and your validation path both work from the repo's documented commands.

If you want a quick manual check, add one command that tells you the app is actually reachable.

```bash
ddev describe
```

This shows the project's running services and local URLs in a readable format. Use it to confirm the container layer is up before you start debugging application code.

## Keep The Workflow Small

You do not need a giant automation layer. You need a few commands that remove repetition, a checked-in environment definition, and one setup path that every contributor can follow.

When you add a new dependency, update the repo-owned workflow at the same time. If you skip that step, your setup drifts back into tribal knowledge.

Ahnii!

[Local-first development](https://www.inkandswitch.com/local-first/) gives you a workflow where your code, tools, and daily progress keep moving on your machine first, which matters if you want faster feedback, fewer fragile dependencies, and a setup you can trust when the network or a hosted service gets in your way.

You feel the difference the first time a remote dependency slows down and your work does not stop.

A local-first setup keeps the important parts close: your source code, your database, your test data, your scripts, and the commands that rebuild the project when something breaks.

That changes how you work.

You spend less time waiting for shared environments to wake up. You spend more time checking real behavior on your machine while the context is still fresh.

Local-first development also makes your project easier to hand to someone else, but only if the setup is clear and repeatable. That is where the rest of the post needs to go next.

## Move the Whole Toolchain in One Pass

When you migrate a toolchain, move the commands, config, and team defaults together so you do not leave your project in a half-old state.

Start with the command your team runs most. If `npm run dev` becomes `pnpm dev`, change the docs, CI, and local scripts in the same pass. That keeps your setup predictable, even on a fresh clone.

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm dev
```

This switches dependency installation and local development to the new toolchain. It also gives you one fast check: a new shell should work without extra fixes.

Then update the files that make the migration stick.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
- name: Install dependencies
  run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

- name: Run tests
  run: pnpm test
```

This moves CI onto the same path your team uses locally. If CI still uses the old commands, your migration is not finished.

---
title: "Write repeatable workflows without sounding like a robot"
date: 2026-04-12
categories: [writing, workflows]
tags: [documentation, process, automation, writing]
summary: "You will learn how to explain a repeatable workflow in clear, varied language that readers can actually follow."
slug: "write-repeatable-workflows-with-rhythm"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to explain a repeatable workflow so your reader can run it the same way every time, and stay awake while they read it.

## Prerequisites

- A workflow with more than one step
- A reader who needs clear instructions, not a story about your process
- A place to put the workflow, such as a README, runbook, or blog post

## Start With the Stable Shape of the Workflow

A repeatable workflow has a fixed path.

Your job is to show that path first.

Do that before you add edge cases, tool choices, or commentary. If the reader cannot see the backbone, the rest turns into noise, but a simple shape gives you room to vary the pace in the next section.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Prepare inputs] --> B[Run the command]
    B --> C[Check the result]
    C --> D[Ship or fix]
```

This diagram gives the reader the full path in one glance. It also keeps you from spending four paragraphs describing a flow that fits in four boxes.

## Turn the Workflow Into Direct Steps

Once you have the shape, write each step as an instruction.

Use verbs.

Keep the subject obvious. If the reader should do the action, say so. That gives the section momentum, but plain verbs alone are still not enough if every line lands with the same beat.

{{< steps >}}
{{< step "Prepare the inputs" >}}
Gather the files, values, or credentials the workflow needs. Put them in one known place so the next step starts clean.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Run one command" >}}
Use a single command or entry point for the main action. Readers should not have to remember a custom sequence from memory.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Verify the result" >}}
Check the output right away. Look for the specific signal that tells you the workflow worked.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Handle the next move" >}}
If verification passes, continue. If it fails, stop and fix the problem before you pile more steps on top.
{{< /step >}}
{{< /steps >}}

The shortcode keeps the sequence visible, and each step earns its place because it tells the reader what to do now. The next problem is tone: clear instructions can still sound flat if every sentence marches at the same speed.

## Vary the Cadence Without Losing Clarity

Short sentences create force.

Medium sentences create flow.

Use both.

If every sentence is clipped, the section starts to bark at the reader. If every sentence stretches out to explain itself, the section drifts and loses pressure.

Compare these two versions:

```markdown
Run the check. Review the output. Fix the errors. Run it again. Ship the change.
```

This version is clear, but the rhythm is too even. Five short hits in a row feel mechanical.

```markdown
Run the check first. Review the output while the context is still fresh, then fix the errors that matter. After that, run it again and ship only when the result stays clean.
```

This version still teaches the same workflow, but it breathes. You keep the instructions direct while giving the reader a more natural pace.

## Show the Workflow in One Real Example

Readers trust a workflow when they can see it in use.

Give them one command. Then show what success looks like.

```bash
./scripts/publish-check.sh
```

This command acts as the single entry point for the workflow. It tells the reader where to start without making them reconstruct the process from scattered notes.

```text
1. Lint passed
2. Links verified
3. Frontmatter valid
4. Ready to publish
```

This output is short on purpose. It shows the signals the reader should look for, without dumping raw terminal noise into the post.

## End Each Section by Pulling the Reader Forward

A section should close with a reason to keep going.

That reason can be a risk, a missing piece, or a practical question. You do not need a dramatic cliffhanger. You need a sentence that opens the next door.

For example, after you explain the steps, point to tone. After you explain tone, point to proof. After you show proof, point to verification in a real environment. That small pull keeps the post moving.

## Verify the Workflow on a Fresh Run

Read the workflow once as a stranger.

Then run it from the top.

If you have to guess, fill in a missing command, or reread a sentence three times, the workflow is still trapped in your head. Tighten the verbs. Cut the filler. Keep the sequence intact.

# Paths of Glory (1957): ★★★★

*Directed by Stanley Kubrick. Starring Kirk Douglas, Ralph Meeker, Adolphe Menjou, George Macready. 88 minutes.*

---

*Paths of Glory* is one of the clearest anti-war films ever made because it understands exactly where to aim its anger. Kubrick is not interested in battlefield heroics. He is interested in the machinery that sends men forward, watches them die, and then punishes the survivors for failing to perform miracles. The film is lean, cold, and brutally focused. It still lands.

The opening trench sequence tells you almost everything you need to know. Kubrick tracks alongside Colonel Dax as he moves through the line, and the camera keeps finding exhausted faces, mud, tight quarters, and men waiting for orders they already know are bad. A few minutes later the assault on the Anthill begins, and Kubrick stages it with remarkable clarity. You understand the objective, you understand why it is hopeless, and you understand the chain of cowardice above the men doing the actual fighting. The combat is not large in scale, but it is tense because every tactical detail is legible.

That clarity carries into the courtroom material, which is where the film becomes truly vicious. The court-martial of the three soldiers is not played as suspense. Their fate is obvious from the moment they are selected. What matters is the ritual. Adolphe Menjou gives one of the film's best performances as General Broulard, a man so polished and reasonable that his moral emptiness almost sneaks past you. George Macready's Mireau is more openly rotten, especially after the failed attack, but Broulard represents the more enduring evil: a system that can explain anything to itself.

Kirk Douglas is excellent because he does not play Dax as a saint. He is brave, furious, intelligent, and still trapped inside the same structure. That gives the film weight. It never pretends one decent officer can redeem the institution around him. The emotional high point comes at the end, when the captured German girl sings to the soldiers in the tavern and the room slowly changes. Hardened men who have spent the whole film being treated like expendable material suddenly look human again. Kubrick earns that scene because he has been so unsentimental up to that point.

As history, the film compresses events and sharpens personalities, but it respects the truth that matters. This is World War I as organized waste, run by class vanity and careerism. If you care about military history, it sends you back to read more about French Army mutinies, failed offensives, and the politics of command. That is a real compliment.

This is essential viewing for anyone interested in war movies, especially if you prefer films that question military mythology instead of feeding it. It is easy to rewatch because it is so precise. Every scene has a purpose. Very few war films are this angry, this controlled, and this honest.

★★★★

---
title: "Turning a Coding Session Into a Blog Draft That People Can Actually Use"
date: 2026-04-12
categories: [cursor]
tags: [ai-assisted-development, writing-workflow, session-notes]
summary: "I turned a coding session into a focused draft by pulling out the real problem, keeping the structure tight, and writing around the decisions that mattered."
slug: "turning-a-coding-session-into-a-blog-draft"
draft: true
---

## The Problem / Context
A lot of coding sessions feel interesting while they are happening and useless once they are over. The terminal scrollback is full of commands, half-finished ideas, and one or two decisions that actually mattered, but none of that is shaped enough to publish.

That was the tension here. I needed a draft that read like a real build log with a point, not a transcript with some markdown headings dropped on top.

## What I Tried / The Approach
The first useful decision was to stop thinking in terms of chronology. A raw session log usually tells the story in the order I discovered things. That is good for debugging. It is usually bad for readers.

So I pulled the session apart into a smaller set of questions:

- What problem was I actually trying to solve?
- Which decision changed the outcome?
- What did I try first that did not hold up?
- What code or commands make the story concrete?
- What is the takeaway someone else can reuse?

That gave me a filter. If a detail helped answer one of those questions, it stayed. If it only showed that I spent twenty minutes poking around, it went away.

I also kept the post narrow. The session prompt was simple: turn a coding session into a blog draft with a problem, approach, solution, and takeaway. That pushed me toward a workflow post about extracting signal from a session, not a vague reflection on AI tools.

Before drafting, I checked the existing post categories and the overlap guidance. The safe move here was to avoid broad framework architecture or generic Docker material and lean into a practical AI-assisted workflow angle. That made `cursor` a reasonable category.

The overlap check in the workflow is simple and worth keeping simple:

```bash
ls /home/jones/dev/blog/content/posts/*/
grep -rl "session" /home/jones/dev/blog/content/posts/
```

I did not need a taxonomy exercise. I needed to know whether this exact angle was already saturated.

From there I built the post around four fixed sections:

1. The problem
2. The approach
3. The solution
4. The takeaway

That structure is useful because it forces compression. If I cannot explain the session inside those four containers, I probably do not have a post yet.

I also wanted the draft to sound like a person who just finished the work. That meant cutting the usual filler. No long preamble. No claims that the process was transformative. No tutorial voice pretending every step was planned from the beginning.

A small example of that cleanup was the front matter. It is mechanical, but it anchors the draft in the actual blog format, so I wrote it early and moved on:

```yaml
---
title: "Turning a Coding Session Into a Blog Draft That People Can Actually Use"
date: 2026-04-12
categories: [cursor]
tags: [ai-assisted-development, writing-workflow, session-notes]
summary: "I turned a coding session into a focused draft by pulling out the real problem, keeping the structure tight, and writing around the decisions that mattered."
slug: "turning-a-coding-session-into-a-blog-draft"
draft: true
---
```

Once that existed, the rest of the work became editorial. I was not deciding what kind of artifact to make anymore. I was deciding what belonged inside it.

## The Solution
The working pattern ended up being straightforward.

First, I identified the real problem statement in plain language. In this case it was not "write a blog post." It was "turn a noisy coding session into a post with a clear arc and enough specifics to be worth reading." That sentence gave the draft a spine.

Second, I selected only the session details that supported that spine. The commands for checking blog overlap mattered. The front matter mattered. The decision to organize the post around the moments that changed the work mattered. A blow-by-blow list of every exploratory step did not.

Third, I wrote the draft around decisions, failed starts, and concrete artifacts. Readers learn more from that than from a polished summary that hides the uncertainty. The wrong turn here was assuming the session itself already had a narrative. It did not. I had to make one by choosing a center of gravity.

That is the core move:

```markdown
## The Problem / Context
State the tension in 2-3 sentences.

## What I Tried / The Approach
Show the filtering, trade-offs, and any wrong turn.

## The Solution
Show the concrete output, commands, or code.

## What I Learned
End with the reusable lesson.
```

That template sounds obvious until you try to use it on real session material. Real sessions are messy. They sprawl. They contain setup noise, repeated checks, and side quests that felt important at the time. The structure works because it gives me permission to cut hard.

I also tried to keep the prose at the same resolution as the work. If I mention a workflow rule, I pair it with an example. If I mention a choice, I name the choice. If I mention a draft, I show the shape of the draft. That keeps the post from drifting into generic commentary.

The final draft became a small, opinionated build log: start with the actual tension, keep the scope tight, show a few real pieces of the workflow, and end with what I would repeat next time.

## What I Learned
A coding session is raw material, not a blog post. Treating the transcript like a first draft usually produces something bloated and flat.

The useful move was to write around the decisions. Once I picked the real problem and a handful of concrete details, the structure did most of the heavy lifting.

I would keep using this approach for session writeups:

- find the problem that created tension
- keep only the steps that changed the outcome
- show a few real commands or snippets
- end with the lesson I would carry into the next session

I would also keep the post focused on one idea. If a session has three interesting arcs, it probably deserves three short posts. One clean post beats one giant recap every time.

This draft is still marked `draft: true`, which is the right default. The shape is there. The next pass is where I would tighten wording, swap in any better examples from the actual session log, and remove anything that feels like it could have been written without doing the work.

Ahnii!

I spent part of this week tightening up the shape of my work instead of adding another layer of noise on top of it. That was the real build session. Not a flashy launch, not a giant feature drop. I sat with the parts of my stack that were starting to drift, especially inside [Waaseyaa](https://waaseyaa.org), and I worked on making the foundation feel like mine again.

## The Problem / The Why

I keep running into the same tension. I want to move fast because there is a lot to build. I have [Minoo](https://minoo.live), I have [OIATC](https://oiatc.waaseyaa.org), I have client work and infrastructure work and all the invisible glue that keeps a small ecosystem standing. But if I move too fast for too long, the code starts to feel borrowed from urgency instead of shaped by intention.

That is usually when I know I need a different kind of session. I need to stop chasing surface progress and look at the structure underneath. I need to ask whether the tools I am building are actually helping me tell the truth of the work. Not in a branding sense. In a practical sense. Can I come back to this code in a week and still know what I was thinking. Can I extend it without fighting it. Can I trust it enough to build community systems on top of it.

That question matters more to me because these projects are not side experiments. They are part of a longer attempt to build Indigenous digital infrastructure that is accountable to place, language, and actual people. If the base is sloppy, everything above it inherits that weakness.

## What I Built / What I Found

This session turned into a cleanup, but not the cosmetic kind. I worked through framework structure, documentation patterns, and the places where my implementation had started to outrun my own thinking. I was pulling pieces back into alignment so the next feature would land in a cleaner system.

A lot of that meant reducing ambiguity. I clarified how certain parts of the framework are supposed to fit together, where responsibilities belong, and what should be treated as stable versus experimental. Some of the work was code. Some of it was naming. Some of it was writing down decisions that had only been living in my head. That part always feels slower than shipping a visible feature, but it saves me later.

What I found, again, is that drift does not usually arrive as one big failure. It shows up as a dozen small compromises. A script that works but does not belong where it lives. A pattern repeated three different ways because I never stopped to consolidate it. A feature that technically runs, but leaves behind confusion for my future self.

I also found that my best sessions lately are the ones where I stop pretending every piece of progress has to look public. Some of the most important work I do is making sure the internal logic of the system stays coherent. That is the difference between building a pile of useful parts and building something that can keep growing.

This is also where the relationship between the projects becomes clearer for me. Waaseyaa is the foundation. Minoo is one expression of what that foundation makes possible. OIATC carries a different community and institutional weight. When I make the core cleaner, I am not just polishing a framework. I am creating better conditions for all the work that depends on it.

## Where It's Going

Next, I want to keep pushing toward stronger defaults and less hidden complexity. I do not want a framework that only makes sense because I remember every compromise that produced it. I want something I can live inside for years. Something that stays readable, adaptable, and grounded.

That also means being more deliberate about what I do not build yet. There are still features I want to chase, and some of them would be fun to show off. But I would rather earn that pace by getting the shape of the system right first. I have done enough hurried building to know the bill always comes due.

I think this is the real story of the work right now. Not scale. Not hype. Just trying to build software with enough clarity that it can carry responsibility.

Follow the build if you want to see where that goes. Subscribe or reply if this kind of slower, grounded progress makes sense to you.

```json
{

  }
}
```

This adds a reusable script to your `composer.json`. You can run `composer build-docs` any time you need a fresh build.

# Configure Your Project

This section shows you how to move from a default install to a working configuration file.

## Create Your Configuration File

Start with a dedicated config file at the root of your project. Keep it small. Add only the values your app needs to boot.

```yaml
app:
  name: Inventory Service
  env: production
  debug: false

database:
  host: localhost
  port: 5432
  name: inventory
  user: inventory_user
  password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
```

This file defines your base application settings. It also keeps secrets out of source control by reading the database password from an environment variable.

## Load Configuration at Startup

Load the file as early as possible. Your app should read config before it opens database connections, registers services, or handles requests.

```php
<?php

use Symfony\Component\Yaml\Yaml;

$config = Yaml::parseFile(__DIR__ . '/config.yaml');

$app = new Application($config);
$app->boot();
```

This code reads `config.yaml` with [Symfony YAML](https://symfony.com/doc/current/components/yaml.html). Then it passes the parsed values into your application during boot.

## Override Values with Environment Variables

Use environment variables for values that change between machines. That usually means secrets, hostnames, and deployment-specific flags.

```php
<?php

$config['database']['password'] = getenv('DB_PASSWORD') ?: $config['database']['password'];
$config['app']['env'] = getenv('APP_ENV') ?: $config['app']['env'];
```

This keeps your committed config stable while still letting each environment supply its own values. You get one source of truth, with a narrow set of safe overrides.

## Validate Required Settings

Fail fast when a required value is missing. A broken config should stop the app before it starts doing work.

```php
<?php

$required = [
    'app.name',
    'database.host',
    'database.name',
    'database.user',
];

foreach ($required as $key) {
    if (! hasConfigValue($config, $key)) {
        throw new RuntimeException("Missing required config value: {$key}");
    }
}
```

This check turns silent misconfiguration into a clear startup error. You find the problem immediately, not halfway through a request.

## Split Local and Production Settings

Keep shared defaults in one file. Put machine-specific values in a second file that is ignored by Git.

```yaml
# config.local.yaml
app:
  debug: true

database:
  host: 127.0.0.1
  name: inventory_local
```

This local file lets you change development settings without touching the base config. Your production defaults stay clean, and your local setup stays flexible.

## Merge Configuration in a Predictable Order

Load files in the same order every time. Defaults first. Local overrides second. Environment variables last.

```php
<?php

$base = Yaml::parseFile(__DIR__ . '/config.yaml');
$local = file_exists(__DIR__ . '/config.local.yaml')
    ? Yaml::parseFile(__DIR__ . '/config.local.yaml')
    : [];

$config = array_replace_recursive($base, $local);
$config['database']['password'] = getenv('DB_PASSWORD') ?: $config['database']['password'];
```

This gives you a clear precedence chain. When a value changes, you know exactly where it came from.

# Package Overview

You use this package to define repeatable application behavior in code. It gives you a clear place to register inputs, run validation, execute handlers, and return consistent output.

## Understand What the Package Does

This package handles one job: it turns a scattered workflow into a single, testable unit. You declare the inputs, define the rules, and let the package run the workflow the same way every time.

You do not need ad hoc validation in controllers, duplicated setup code, or custom response formatting in multiple places. You keep the workflow in one package boundary and call it where you need it.

## Use the Package in Your Application

You add the package when a feature has the same shape every time: accept input, check rules, perform work, return a result. That keeps your application code smaller and easier to follow.

You can use it for background jobs, admin actions, API operations, or internal service calls. If the workflow needs clear inputs and predictable output, this package fits.

## Keep Behavior Consistent

The package helps you enforce one execution path. Your validation rules run before the main handler. Your handler receives clean data. Your result comes back in a format your application can rely on.

That consistency matters when the same operation runs in more than one place. You write the workflow once and reuse it across HTTP requests, CLI commands, and queued work.

## Test the Workflow Directly

You can test the package at the workflow level. Pass in input, assert on validation, and check the returned result.

That gives you faster tests and clearer failures. You do not need to boot an entire request cycle just to verify one operation.

## Fit the Package Into a Larger Codebase

This package works best when you want application rules to live outside controllers and templates. You keep transport code thin and move feature logic into something you can read, test, and change without hunting through the stack.

If your current code mixes validation, side effects, and response handling in one file, this package gives you a cleaner split. You define the workflow once. Your application calls it where needed.
